screens.title: Secure Shell (SSH) — Configuration & Hardening
screens.narratorSegment: SSH is the fundamental encrypted channel you use every time you administer a Linux server remotely. In this lesson we'll focus on configuring SSH so it reduces risk rather than increasing it. You will learn why key-based authentication is stronger than passwords, how the SSH daemon reads settings from /etc/ssh/sshd_config, and which server- and client-side adjustments give you better security and usability. We'll also cover practical precautions: always test key access before disabling passwords, keep a recovery session open while you change settings, and verify file permissions for ~/. ssh and authorized_keys. A concrete example you will practice is generating an ed25519 key pair, copying the public key to a server, and then editing sshd_config to disable password authentication and block direct root login. A common misconception is that changing the SSH port or disabling password auth alone makes SSH invulnerable; these steps reduce noisy scans and brute-force hits but are part of layered defense. By the end of this chapter you'll be able to implement a repeatable hardening checklist and recover safely if a change locks you out. screens.title: Learning Objectives — Practical Verification
screens.narratorSegment: Knowing which settings to change is only half the job; verifying behavior and keeping a recovery path is the other half. This objective screen focuses on practical verification steps you must take after any SSH change. For example, after you install your public key on a server, test logging in from a new terminal that does not already have an authenticated agent. If you plan to disable PasswordAuthentication, first confirm that key-based login works and keep an existing session open. When you change sshd_config, restart the service with sudo systemctl restart sshd and then test from a separate connection using the intended port and identity file. Also verify file permissions: ~/. ssh should be chmod 700 and authorized_keys chmod 600. Misconceptions often arise when administrators use reload instead of restart, or when they forget to specify the identity file and see an unexpected authentication prompt. Each objective here ends with a small verification action: log in from a new terminal, check service status, and confirm permission bits. These checks prevent lockouts and give you confidence the server remains accessible after hardening.

screens.title: What is SSH and why it matters
screens.narratorSegment: SSH, or Secure Shell, is a cryptographic network protocol that creates an encrypted channel between a client and a remote server. At its simplest, SSH guarantees confidentiality and integrity for remote command execution and file transfers so that credentials and commands are not exposed to eavesdroppers. A practical example: when you log into a cloud server to update packages, SSH prevents anyone on the same network from sniffing your password or session. SSH also supports multiple authentication methods—passwords, public keys, and agent-based forwarding—and additional features like port forwarding and X11 forwarding. A frequent misconception is assuming SSH encryption alone is enough; while SSH protects the channel, server configuration and account controls determine who can connect. For example, leaving root login enabled or allowing password authentication increases risk even when using SSH. Key takeaway: SSH secures the transport, but correct configuration and key management complete the security story. To test your understanding, explain which authentication method you would choose for automated backups and why. What is SSH and why it matters means ssh provides an encrypted channel for remote administration and file transfer, but proper configuration controls who can use it.. In practical terms, definition, practical purpose, and real-world example. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Core Concept
What is SSH and why it matters
Secure remote shell with encrypted communications and extensible authentication.
  • Provides encrypted login and remote command execution.
  • Supports key-based auth for stronger, passwordless logins.
  • Enables secure file transfer and port forwarding features.
Example
Use SSH to run package updates on a remote server without exposing your password over the network.
Key commands
ssh-keygen -t ed25519 -C "my_secure_key"
ssh-copy-id -i ~/.ssh/id_ed25519.pub your_user@your_server
ssh your_user@your_server
Common mistake
Relying only on SSH encryption while leaving weak account controls in place.
Key takeaway
SSH is secure transport; account and server settings enforce who can reach you.

screens.title: Generating SSH keys with ssh-keygen
screens.narratorSegment: Generating a key pair is the first practical step toward key-based authentication. The ssh-keygen utility creates a private key that you keep secret and a public key you place on servers. A recommended modern command uses ed25519 for compact strong keys: ssh-keygen -t ed25519 -C "my_secure_key". When prompted, accept the default file path in ~/. ssh and set a strong passphrase to protect the private key at rest. A passphrase is not the same as a login password: it encrypts your private key on disk so that if the file is stolen, the attacker still needs the passphrase. After generation, you will have two files, for example id_ed25519 and id_ed25519. pub. The public key is safe to copy; the private key must never be shared. A common misconception is that an empty passphrase is acceptable for convenience; this exposes you to risk if the machine storing the private key is compromised. Example: create the key, then inspect permissions and ensure ~/. ssh is 700. Closing question: what tradeoffs do you accept if you decide not to use a passphrase on an automated backup key?

content.html:
Process
Generating SSH keys with ssh-keygen
Recommended command
ssh-keygen -t ed25519 -C "my_secure_key"
# Accept default location: ~/.ssh/id_ed25519
# Enter a strong passphrase when prompted
After generation you'll see two files: id_ed25519 (private) and id_ed25519.pub (public). Keep the private file secure and readable only by you.
Why passphrases matter
A passphrase encrypts the private key on disk. If your laptop is stolen, the key file alone is not enough to authenticate without the passphrase.
Common mistake
Using an empty passphrase for convenience increases risk; prefer an agent like ssh-agent for usability instead.
Example
Generate an ed25519 key for admin tasks and protect it with a memorable but strong passphrase stored in your password manager.
Key takeaway
Prefer modern algorithms and always protect private keys; use agents for convenience.

screens.title: Deploying public keys to a server
screens.narratorSegment: Copying your public key to a remote server is the deployment step that allows key-based login. The ssh-copy-id utility automates appending your public key to the remote user's ~/. ssh/authorized_keys and sets safe permissions. For example, run ssh-copy-id -i ~/. ssh/id_ed25519. pub your_user@your_server_ip and enter the user's password for that session. After copying, verify you can authenticate from a new terminal using ssh your_user@your_server_ip and that you are prompted for the key passphrase rather than the account password. If you cannot authenticate, common issues include incorrect permissions on ~/. ssh (must be 700) or authorized_keys (must be 600) or the public key being corrupted during copy. If you don't have ssh-copy-id, you can manually append the public key to ~/. ssh/authorized_keys and then set permissions with chmod 700 ~/. ssh and chmod 600 ~/. ssh/authorized_keys. A misconception is that authorized_keys can be group- or world-readable; SSH refuses such permissive settings. Key takeaway: automated tools reduce mistakes, but always confirm permissions and test from a separate session so you don't lose access. Deploying public keys to a server means use ssh-copy-id or manual append plus strict permissions to ensure the server accepts your public key.. In practical terms, use ssh-copy-id and verify authorized_keys and permissions. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Process Flow
Deploying public keys to a server
Preferred method
ssh-copy-id -i ~/.ssh/id_ed25519.pub your_user@your_server_ip
# Enter remote user's password when prompted
# Then test: ssh your_user@your_server_ip
Manual method
cat ~/.ssh/id_ed25519.pub | ssh your_user@server 'mkdir -p ~/.ssh && cat >> ~/.ssh/authorized_keys'
# Then on server:
chmod 700 ~/.ssh
chmod 600 ~/.ssh/authorized_keys
Example
Use ssh-copy-id when possible to avoid subtle formatting errors in authorized_keys.
Common mistake
Incorrect permissions on ~/.ssh or authorized_keys cause publickey authentication to fail.
Key takeaway
Always verify login from a new terminal and enforce strict permission bits.

screens.title: sshd_config — the server control file
screens.narratorSegment: The sshd daemon reads its operational settings from /etc/ssh/sshd_config, and those directives determine who can connect and how. Important directives include Port to change the listening port, PermitRootLogin to allow or disallow direct root sign-in, PasswordAuthentication to enable or disable password logins, AllowUsers and AllowGroups to whitelist accounts, and X11Forwarding when graphical forwarding is undesired. Changing these settings requires a restart of the sshd service to apply them; sudo systemctl restart sshd is the common command. A common pitfall is editing sshd_config and assuming settings take effect without restarting or testing. Another frequent error is locking out access by changing the port or disabling passwords before verifying key-based connections. For example, setting PasswordAuthentication no and PermitRootLogin no reduces attack surface, but you must first confirm that your user key authenticates and that any automation that relied on passwords has a replacement. A useful habit is to keep a documented backup: sudo cp /etc/ssh/sshd_config /etc/ssh/sshd_config. bak before editing, and keep one session active while testing. What backup and rollback steps will you perform before editing sshd_config on a production node? sshd_config — the server control file means sshd_config centralizes server policies; change it deliberately, back it up, test from another session, and restart sshd to apply.. In practical terms, key directives that change authentication and access. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: sshd_config control
keyIdea.text: sshd_config centralizes server policies; change it deliberately, back it up, test from another session, and restart sshd to apply.

content.html:
Configuration
sshd_config — the server control file
Common directives
# Change port
Port 22222

# Disable root login
PermitRootLogin no

# Disable password authentication
PasswordAuthentication no

# Allow specific users
AllowUsers user1 user2

# Disable X11 forwarding if unused
X11Forwarding no
Practical checklist
  1. Backup sshd_config: sudo cp /etc/ssh/sshd_config /etc/ssh/sshd_config.bak
  2. Edit and save the file.
  3. Restart sshd: sudo systemctl restart sshd
  4. Test from a new terminal before closing existing sessions.
Example
Move SSH to port 22222 and disable root logins for a reduced attack surface.
Common mistake
Disabling password auth before confirming key access, causing lockouts.
Key takeaway
Edit carefully, back up, restart sshd, and validate from a separate connection.

screens.title: Password vs Key-Based Authentication
screens.narratorSegment: Comparing password and key-based authentication clarifies why administrators choose keys for production servers. Password authentication requires the server to verify a secret you type; it is convenient but vulnerable to brute-force attacks and network interception when used improperly. Key-based authentication uses a public-private key pair: the client proves possession of the private key during the handshake, and the server validates the matching public key stored in authorized_keys. Keys remove password guessing and can be paired with passphrases for theft protection. However, passwords are still used for initial setup or on systems where key management is impractical. A misconception is thinking keys eliminate all risk; if private keys are stored without a passphrase or on shared machines, they become a single point of failure. Example scenario: for automated backups running from a trusted host, an admin might use a dedicated key with restricted commands and no passphrase, but only after evaluating physical security and limiting that key's permissions on the server. Key takeaway: prefer key-based authentication with passphrases and least-privilege use for any automation. In practical terms, why keys are preferred and when passwords remain used. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. content.html:
Comparison
Password vs Key-Based Authentication
Password Authentication
  • Easy to set up but vulnerable to brute-force attacks.
  • Requires users to remember or store passwords.
  • Simpler for one-off access or where key management is not available.
Key-Based Authentication
  • Uses cryptographic keys; resists guessing attacks.
  • Private key should be protected with a passphrase and agent for usability.
  • Supports fine-grained controls and restricted keys for automation.
Example
Use a dedicated key for automated tasks and restrict its authorized_keys command= option on the server.
Misconception
Keys are not safe if private files have weak permissions or no passphrase.
Key takeaway
Prefer keys for admins, and manage passphrases and agent use to combine security and convenience.

screens.title: Hardening steps in sshd_config
screens.narratorSegment: Hardening sshd_config is about reducing exposure while preserving necessary access. Start by backing up the file, then apply a minimal, tested set of directives: change Port to a high, non-standard value to avoid noisy scans; set PermitRootLogin no to prevent direct root sessions; set PasswordAuthentication no after confirming key logins; use AllowUsers or AllowGroups to restrict who may connect; disable X11Forwarding if you do not need graphical forwarding; and set LoginGraceTime to a short interval like 30s to limit the window for brute-force attempts. Each choice has tradeoffs: changing the port is security by obscurity but reduces automated scanning noise; restricting users requires managing the allow list; and shortening LoginGraceTime may impact slow networks. After editing, restart sshd and verify access from a new terminal. Always retain a recovery path such as console access or an open session. A common misconception is thinking a single directive will make SSH fully secure; instead, combine multiple small controls to form layered protection. Your action item: write a short checklist to run before and after editing sshd_config on a production host. Hardening steps in sshd_config means combine directives—port change, disable root, disable passwords, limit users, and tighten grace time—then restart and validate.. In practical terms, apply a minimal set of directives for most servers. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Hardening steps in sshd_config
Suggested directives

Port 22222
PermitRootLogin no

screens.title: Restarting sshd and verifying changes
screens.narratorSegment: Applying sshd configuration changes requires restarting or reloading the sshd service. The recommended command is sudo systemctl restart sshd, which fully restarts the service and ensures new settings are active. In some systems sudo systemctl reload sshd may not apply all directives reliably. Best practice is to make a backup of /etc/ssh/sshd_config, open an alternate terminal, and then restart sshd so you can immediately test the new configuration. After restarting, attempt to connect from the new terminal using the intended identity and port, for example ssh -p 22222 -i ~/. ssh/id_ed25519 user@server. If the connection fails and you still have the recovery session, revert the config from the backup. A common misconception is assuming restart is dangerous; when you keep one session active and test from another, restarts are safe and necessary. Example steps include backing up the file, restarting the service, checking sudo systemctl status sshd for errors, and then testing login. Key question: what will you do if systemctl status shows a configuration parsing error after restart? screens.title: Managing ~/.ssh/config for usability and safety
screens.narratorSegment: The client-side file ~/. ssh/config improves usability and reduces mistakes by storing per-host settings and identity mappings. With entries like Host mywebserver, Hostname 192.168.1.100, User webadmin, Port 22222, and IdentityFile ~/. ssh/id_rsa_webserver you can simply ssh mywebserver instead of typing a long command. Client Config
Managing ~/.ssh/config for usability and safety
Example host block
Host mywebserver
    Hostname 192.168.1.100
    User webadmin
    Port 22222
    IdentityFile ~/.ssh/id_rsa_webserver

Type ssh mywebserver to connect with the right port and identity file without remembering details.

Committing private keys or leaving them with permissive permissions accessible to others.

Client config streamlines secure access and prevents human error when multiple hosts and keys are involved.

screens.title: Common SSH mistakes and how to fix them
screens.narratorSegment: When key-based authentication fails, the cause is often a few well-known mistakes. SSH is strict about permission bits: ~/. ssh should be chmod 700 and ~/. ssh/authorized_keys chmod 600. If permissions are more permissive, sshd will ignore authorized_keys and give you a publickey error. Another frequent mistake is disabling PasswordAuthentication before confirming key login; this can lock you out unless you have console access or another way to log in. A typical recovery path is to use your recovery session to restore the backup sshd_config or correct permissions and then restart sshd. Use sudo journalctl -u sshd or sudo systemctl status sshd to inspect errors after a restart—parsing errors will show up there. For permission errors, correct file modes and test again. For automation, consider deploying a temporary sudo-enabled user with console access or leveraging the hosting provider's web console to recover. Key takeaway: always prepare a rollback plan and verify each step from a separate terminal. To practice, intentionally fix an authorized_keys permission issue on a test server and document your recovery steps. In practical terms, permission issues, premature password disable, and recovery steps. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. Troubleshooting
Common SSH mistakes and how to fix them
Permission fixes
chmod 700 ~/.ssh

# Then test key login again
Service & logs

A common trap is assuming one change suffices; security comes from layered, tested controls. Keep a recovery session when you restart sshd and use logs and permission checks to troubleshoot issues. These ideas together form a repeatable checklist that reduces the risk of lockouts and unauthorized access.

fullNarratorScript:
SSH is the fundamental encrypted channel you use every time you administer a Linux server remotely. In this lesson we'll focus on configuring SSH so it reduces risk rather than increasing it. You will learn why key-based authentication is stronger than passwords, how the SSH daemon reads settings from /etc/ssh/sshd_config, and which server- and client-side adjustments give you better security and usability. We'll also cover practical precautions: always test key access before disabling passwords, keep a recovery session open while you change settings, and verify file permissions for ~/. ssh and authorized_keys. A concrete example you will practice is generating an ed25519 key pair, copying the public key to a server, and then editing sshd_config to disable password authentication and block direct root login. A common misconception is that changing the SSH port or disabling password auth alone makes SSH invulnerable; these steps reduce noisy scans and brute-force hits but are part of layered defense. By the end of this chapter you'll be able to implement a repeatable hardening checklist and recover safely if a change locks you out. How will you verify your changes in a new terminal before closing your original session?

By the end of this chapter you'll be able to explain SSH's role, configure key-based authentication, harden the SSH daemon, and manage client settings for secure, repeatable access. First, you'll learn what SSH protects and why encrypted channels matter for remote administration and file transfer. Second, you'll generate key pairs and deploy public keys so you can authenticate without passwords, lowering the risk of brute-force compromise. Third, you'll edit /etc/ssh/sshd_config to enforce security policies such as disabling direct root login, limiting users, and choosing a non-standard port. Fourth, you'll manage client-side ~/. ssh/config entries for safer, concise connections and automated identity selection. Each objective includes a practical verification step: test key login before turning off passwords, keep a recovery session open when restarting sshd, and confirm ~/. ssh permissions are strict. A common misconception is that a single change, like moving SSH to a different port, is sufficient; instead, these objectives form a layered defense where each part reduces risk and improves operational safety. These skills matter because remote access is how administrators operate servers, and securing it prevents both automated and targeted intrusions.

Knowing which settings to change is only half the job; verifying behavior and keeping a recovery path is the other half. This objective screen focuses on practical verification steps you must take after any SSH change. For example, after you install your public key on a server, test logging in from a new terminal that does not already have an authenticated agent. If you plan to disable PasswordAuthentication, first confirm that key-based login works and keep an existing session open. When you change sshd_config, restart the service with sudo systemctl restart sshd and then test from a separate connection using the intended port and identity file. Also verify file permissions: ~/. ssh should be chmod 700 and authorized_keys chmod 600. Misconceptions often arise when administrators use reload instead of restart, or when they forget to specify the identity file and see an unexpected authentication prompt. Each objective here ends with a small verification action: log in from a new terminal, check service status, and confirm permission bits. These checks prevent lockouts and give you confidence the server remains accessible after hardening.

SSH, or Secure Shell, is a cryptographic network protocol that creates an encrypted channel between a client and a remote server. At its simplest, SSH guarantees confidentiality and integrity for remote command execution and file transfers so that credentials and commands are not exposed to eavesdroppers. A practical example: when you log into a cloud server to update packages, SSH prevents anyone on the same network from sniffing your password or session. SSH also supports multiple authentication methods—passwords, public keys, and agent-based forwarding—and additional features like port forwarding and X11 forwarding. A frequent misconception is assuming SSH encryption alone is enough; while SSH protects the channel, server configuration and account controls determine who can connect. For example, leaving root login enabled or allowing password authentication increases risk even when using SSH. Key takeaway: SSH secures the transport, but correct configuration and key management complete the security story. To test your understanding, explain which authentication method you would choose for automated backups and why. What is SSH and why it matters means ssh provides an encrypted channel for remote administration and file transfer, but proper configuration controls who can use it.. In practical terms, definition, practical purpose, and real-world example. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Generating a key pair is the first practical step toward key-based authentication. The ssh-keygen utility creates a private key that you keep secret and a public key you place on servers. A recommended modern command uses ed25519 for compact strong keys: ssh-keygen -t ed25519 -C "my_secure_key". When prompted, accept the default file path in ~/. ssh and set a strong passphrase to protect the private key at rest. A passphrase is not the same as a login password: it encrypts your private key on disk so that if the file is stolen, the attacker still needs the passphrase. After generation, you will have two files, for example id_ed25519 and id_ed25519. pub. The public key is safe to copy; the private key must never be shared. A common misconception is that an empty passphrase is acceptable for convenience; this exposes you to risk if the machine storing the private key is compromised. Example: create the key, then inspect permissions and ensure ~/. ssh is 700. Closing question: what tradeoffs do you accept if you decide not to use a passphrase on an automated backup key?

Copying your public key to a remote server is the deployment step that allows key-based login. The ssh-copy-id utility automates appending your public key to the remote user's ~/. ssh/authorized_keys and sets safe permissions. For example, run ssh-copy-id -i ~/. ssh/id_ed25519. pub your_user@your_server_ip and enter the user's password for that session. After copying, verify you can authenticate from a new terminal using ssh your_user@your_server_ip and that you are prompted for the key passphrase rather than the account password. If you cannot authenticate, common issues include incorrect permissions on ~/. ssh (must be 700) or authorized_keys (must be 600) or the public key being corrupted during copy. If you don't have ssh-copy-id, you can manually append the public key to ~/. ssh/authorized_keys and then set permissions with chmod 700 ~/. ssh and chmod 600 ~/. ssh/authorized_keys. A misconception is that authorized_keys can be group- or world-readable; SSH refuses such permissive settings. Key takeaway: automated tools reduce mistakes, but always confirm permissions and test from a separate session so you don't lose access. Deploying public keys to a server means use ssh-copy-id or manual append plus strict permissions to ensure the server accepts your public key.. In practical terms, use ssh-copy-id and verify authorized_keys and permissions. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

The sshd daemon reads its operational settings from /etc/ssh/sshd_config, and those directives determine who can connect and how. Important directives include Port to change the listening port, PermitRootLogin to allow or disallow direct root sign-in, PasswordAuthentication to enable or disable password logins, AllowUsers and AllowGroups to whitelist accounts, and X11Forwarding when graphical forwarding is undesired. Changing these settings requires a restart of the sshd service to apply them; sudo systemctl restart sshd is the common command. A common pitfall is editing sshd_config and assuming settings take effect without restarting or testing. Another frequent error is locking out access by changing the port or disabling passwords before verifying key-based connections. For example, setting PasswordAuthentication no and PermitRootLogin no reduces attack surface, but you must first confirm that your user key authenticates and that any automation that relied on passwords has a replacement. A useful habit is to keep a documented backup: sudo cp /etc/ssh/sshd_config /etc/ssh/sshd_config. bak before editing, and keep one session active while testing. In practical terms, key directives that change authentication and access. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. Comparing password and key-based authentication clarifies why administrators choose keys for production servers. Password authentication requires the server to verify a secret you type; it is convenient but vulnerable to brute-force attacks and network interception when used improperly. Key-based authentication uses a public-private key pair: the client proves possession of the private key during the handshake, and the server validates the matching public key stored in authorized_keys. Keys remove password guessing and can be paired with passphrases for theft protection. However, passwords are still used for initial setup or on systems where key management is impractical. A misconception is thinking keys eliminate all risk; if private keys are stored without a passphrase or on shared machines, they become a single point of failure. Example scenario: for automated backups running from a trusted host, an admin might use a dedicated key with restricted commands and no passphrase, but only after evaluating physical security and limiting that key's permissions on the server. Key takeaway: prefer key-based authentication with passphrases and least-privilege use for any automation. Applying sshd configuration changes requires restarting or reloading the sshd service. The recommended command is sudo systemctl restart sshd, which fully restarts the service and ensures new settings are active. In some systems sudo systemctl reload sshd may not apply all directives reliably. Best practice is to make a backup of /etc/ssh/sshd_config, open an alternate terminal, and then restart sshd so you can immediately test the new configuration. If the connection fails and you still have the recovery session, revert the config from the backup. When key-based authentication fails, the cause is often a few well-known mistakes. SSH is strict about permission bits: ~/. ssh should be chmod 700 and ~/. ssh/authorized_keys chmod 600. If permissions are more permissive, sshd will ignore authorized_keys and give you a publickey error. Another frequent mistake is disabling PasswordAuthentication before confirming key login; this can lock you out unless you have console access or another way to log in. A typical recovery path is to use your recovery session to restore the backup sshd_config or correct permissions and then restart sshd. Use sudo journalctl -u sshd or sudo systemctl status sshd to inspect errors after a restart—parsing errors will show up there. For permission errors, correct file modes and test again. For automation, consider deploying a temporary sudo-enabled user with console access or leveraging the hosting provider's web console to recover. These are the core concepts to keep in mind. First, SSH provides encrypted remote access, but encryption alone doesn't enforce who may connect; sshd_config does. Second, key-based authentication replaces passwords with cryptographic key pairs; protect private keys with passphrases and strict permissions. Third, server hardening—changing the port, disabling root and passwords, limiting users, and shortening LoginGraceTime—reduces exposure when applied safely and tested. Each concept pairs with a practical habit: back up sshd_config before edits, verify key logins from a separate terminal, and use ~/. ssh/config for safe, repeatable client connections. A common trap is assuming one change suffices; security comes from layered, tested controls. Keep a recovery session when you restart sshd and use logs and permission checks to troubleshoot issues. These ideas together form a repeatable checklist that reduces the risk of lockouts and unauthorized access.

Keep three compact reminders for daily operations. First, always prefer key-based authentication for administrative accounts and protect private keys with passphrases. Second, make small, tested changes in /etc/ssh/sshd_config—back up before editing, restart the daemon, and validate from a separate terminal to avoid lockouts. Third, manage client-side settings in ~/. ssh/config to choose the correct identity file and reduce human errors.
